subtopic: TARIFF OF FEES FOR INSPECTION OF CANNED FISH AND SHELL FISH

speechtext:
Hon. GROTE STIRLING (Acting Minister of Fisheries) moved the second reading of Bill No. 25, to amend the Meat and Canned Foods Act.
Mr. NEILL Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
subtopic: TARIFF OF FEES FOR INSPECTION OF CANNED FISH AND SHELL FISH
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this amending bill is to make quite sure that power does exist under the statute to charge fees for inspection. There is no doubt that under section 18 of the Meat and Canned Foods Act fish and shellfish packed in cans shall be inspected. There is no doubt that under section 26 of the regulations under this act provision is made for that inspection, and there is no doubt that under section 20 of the regulations a fee is prescribed, but there is doubt as to whether there is power in the act to collect that fee. Therefore the purpose of this amending bill is to make sure that the measure contains a specific statutory provision, and that is its only purpose.

subtopic: TARIFF OF FEES FOR INSPECTION OF CANNED FISH AND SHELL FISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the resolution preceding this bill was in committee, at page 1438 of Hansard the minister was kind enough to indicate his willingness to send it to the marine and fisheries committee. The right hon. gentleman who was leading the government at the time, however, suggested that there was no reason for doing so, as it was merely a formal matter, but I pointed out that it goes further than that. The explanatory note in the bill states:
Section 20 of these regulations provides for a fee for inspection at the rate of one cent per case. The fee is a reasonable one, and at present covers only the cost of inspection.
One reason I should have liked to see the bill go to the marine and fisheries committee is that I challenge both those statements. I say the fee is not reasonable and that it should not be imposed at all. The fee is high, and is not appropriate. Perhaps I am repeating

something I have said previously, but the point is this. I cannot find any other raw product or semi-manufactured product in any other part of Canada in connection with which the person who produces the article has to pay a high fee for its inspection. I think an appropriate parallel would be that of lobsters. If the minister is prepared to show that the lobster people in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick pay a high fee for the inspection of their lobsters it might be a parallel case, but that is not so. The only inspection that takes place in that connection is the inspection of the canneries, which is carried on by officials paid by the government, so the procedure here is entirely different.
There are three main objectionable features to tills inspection fee. In the first place the canneries themselves appoint the inspectors. That statement may be challenged; technically, they do not appoint them but practically they do, because they recommend who shall be appointed. Is that not much the same thing? So we have the extraordinary situation of the government deciding that a certain product shall be inspected, in order to encourage its marketing and sale. I quite admit that this is necessary, but then they say to the people who put up that product, "You name somebody to inspect it and we will appoint them." This method is unworkable, as I predicted it would be, for a dozen different reasons. The next feature is that the cannery men have to pay for this inspection. Why? Do the people whose cheese, butter or meat is inspected have to pay a special fee? No, it comes out of the consolidated revenue fund, so why should the cannery men ibe mulcted to this extent? There is a further considerable tax placed upon them in this way; quite a large quantity of their tinned goods must be opened and destroyed, and that is quite an appreciable addition to the cost of packing. Under the Meat and Canned Foods Act, in connection with other canned foods such as vegetables it is the duty of the inspector to prowl around the cannery to see that sanitary conditions are all right, that the articles put up, vegetables for instance, are fresh and sound, to see that any colouring matter used is correct chemically and so on. Then in his discretion the inspector may open certain tins, but the suggestion of the act is that most of the inspection takes place in connection with the operation of the cannery.
That is not so in regard to salmon canning. The regulations tare very strict; they say that out of fifty cases the inspector must take so many, I think twelve. Out of 101 oases he must take eighteen, from 501 to 1,000 cases

Meat and Canned Foods Act
he must take' twenty-four, and so on. They must be taken out of that particular lot offered for inspection, and if the cannery happens to be doing business in a small way, not selling 50,000 oases at a time but drawing out only perhaps 100 oases, the cannery must pay dearly, because the expense is greater in proportion. One tin is taken out of each of these cases and opened, and of course the contents are a total loss. In a cannery putting up 100,000 cases the loss, according to whether he took it out in large or small lots, would run from $6,000 down to $1,100. Then, he has to pay a cent a case, and on a pack of 100,000 cases this item alone amounts to $1,000. I submit that it is an improper tax; it is not a fee. I say it is a heavy tax.
Then further, the statement is made that the fee is reasonable; I say the fee is not reasonable. I figured it out on the amount of salmon canned in British Columbia. Out there five inspectors are appointed, but only three do the work. Those three have power if necessary to call in the other two. They are paid by the case, however, and we may be sure there would not be much danger of the other two men being called in. It is only natural, human nature being what it is, to keep as much of the money in one's own hands as possible. So hon. members will understand that the fees are divided among three men, and in that way they receive sums much greater than those which would be appropriate or even necessary. For much smaller sums we could get men to devote their whole time to the work. The inspectors I have mentioned do not guarantee to spend their whole time or even a considerable portion of it; they simply agree to do the inspecting. In addition they carry on lucrative businesses. I may add there is even the suggestion that they are interested in competitive business. For the moment however we shall let that matter pass. At any rate they are acting as brokers, and are being paid on the basis of so much a case, with the result that their remuneration comes to an amount much greater than is necessary, and much greater than need be paid.
I feel this matter might be more easily debated in committee, upon which occasion the arguments I have advanced might be answered. I point particularly however to the lobster industry and to the industry connected with dry salt herring, and the inspections in connection therewith. Have the people in those industries had to pay for that inspection? No, the government inspector does that work. Then, why should the canneries, which for various reasons seem to be running in hard luck, be singled out to be mulcted first by
having an unusually large number of their tins destroyed and then by having to pay inspection fees? I believe they will be quite willing to stand the loss of tins, and possibly it would be proper to ask them to do so, but I do not know why they should have to pay this inspection fee, one which is not paid in any other parallel industry in Canada.
I suggest the minister should consider the arguments I have advanced. They may be combatable-I do not know-but so far I have not heard any answer. I do suggest however that we would do well to allow the matter to go to the marine and fisheries committee.

subtopic: TARIFF OF FEES FOR INSPECTION OF CANNED FISH AND SHELL FISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the minister
closes the debate may I say that I cannot understand why the fisheries must be subject to all sorts of restrictions, taxes and fees. It seems to me that the officials of the department in the Hunter building must sit up nights trying to find ways and means to discourage the fishermen, the packers and the canners from carrying on their legitimate occupation. Why should there be any fees in connection with canned fish and shellfish any more than with canned tomatoes or canned peaches? Why should the department ask the house to place a fee on canned fish and shellfish? How are they going to make their decisions so far as shellfish are concerned?-because that would mean fish on the shell, not in cans. How could an inspector tell anything about them? Could the minister explain that? I am afraid hs is like other ministers who have preceded him; they do not know what it is all about. It is about time we had a shake-up in the fisheries department; that department should not continue to discourage this great industry, one more capable of development than any other industry in Canada. The officials of the department are trying to place all kinds of restrictions and regulations in the way, and the result is that people get tired of it all and will not invest their money in the industry. I say to the minister that there is only one thing to do with Bill No. 26, and that is not to proceed with it, because it is not in the interests of the fisheries. Why should there be any fee on canned fish? It is all right to have officials going around and inspecting them, but even then it is impossible to carry on a proper inspection. I don't object to the fishermen having to take out licences, but I do object to them having to pay a licence fee.

subtopic: TARIFF OF FEES FOR INSPECTION OF CANNED FISH AND SHELL FISH
speechtext: It looks fishy to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
subtopic: TARIFF OF FEES FOR INSPECTION OF CANNED FISH AND SHELL FISH
speechtext: I am surprised to hear any hon. member advance the view that an inspection of articles of trade should not be undertaken.

subtopic: TARIFF OF FEES FOR INSPECTION OF CANNED FISH AND SHELL FISH
speechtext:
I did not say that. I said
that the man who bought fish should be the man to inspect them, not some official 
appointed either for political or for other purposes who would1 not know whether a fish was good or bad.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
subtopic: TARIFF OF FEES FOR INSPECTION OF CANNED FISH AND SHELL FISH
speechtext: I repeat that in the early part of his remarks the hon. member said that in any case the inspection was bad-

subtopic: TARIFF OF FEES FOR INSPECTION OF CANNED FISH AND SHELL FISH
speechtext: No. I said it was inadequate.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
subtopic: TARIFF OF FEES FOR INSPECTION OF CANNED FISH AND SHELL FISH
speechtext:
-and should not be undertaken by the department. The inspection to which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has referred is one which has been discussed and considered by the trade concerned for a good many years. Various methods of inspection have been attempted; some have been discarded, and others to which reference has been made have for the last few years been carried on, as I maintain, successfully. There is a difference of opinion on the subject; there is a difference of opinion on most of these subjects, and I quite agree with the hon. member for Cornox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) that possibly the way to thresh it out and give everybody an opportunity of being heard is for the bill to go to the fisheries committee. I have no objection to that. Everybody will have an opportunity to ventilate his views there, even my hon. friend who does not agree with inspection at all, and after the second reading I shall be glad so to move.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 POWER TO PRESCRIBE PEES FOR FISHERY LICENCES
speechtext: I do not think it is fair or right that a lobster fisherman or any fisherman should have to pay a licence fee. I do not object to t'heir having to take out a licence so that the department can have a record of those fishing and the quantity of fish caught, but I do not think it is right or fair that a fisherman should have to pay a licence fee any more than the man who grows cabbages or cuts dowm trees in the woods should have to pay a licence fee. Why should the men who go out on the Atlantic or on the Pacific or on the great lakes and risk their lives, their boats and their gear have to pay a licence fee to the Fisheries department? I do not object to their 'having to take out a licence so that the department can compile statistics at the end of the year, although to my mind they are not very valuable, because they are not correct; but I do object, as I always have done, to these fishermen having to pay twenty-five cents or a dollar for a licence, or whatever fee the department charges. Anyone who looks into t'he fisheries regulations will see that the department is operating under regulations made by itself and not prescribed
Fisheries Act

under an act of this parliament. If the minister finds it necessary at the present time to bring in a bill to make it legal to collect these fees from the fishermen, it is only fair to assume that a great many af the other acts which the department is doing by regulation are also illegal.

Mr. MaoLEAN: That is one of the points I tried to bring to the attention of the house last night, that the Department of Fisheries has no right under any statute of this country to lease oyster areas, and that it is being done under the department's own regulations. speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 POWER TO PRESCRIBE PEES FOR FISHERY LICENCES
speechtext: As I have already pointed out, it appears as if these fees, which have been collected for many years, have not been supported by definite words in the Fisheries Act. That is recognized and now it is being corrected. The view expressed by the Deputy Minister of Justice may be explained as follows. The amendments are made to clear up any possible doubt that anyone may have as to the legality of the action taken by the governor in council in imposing fees for certain services. maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 POWER TO PRESCRIBE PEES FOR FISHERY LICENCES
speechtext:
In what the minister has read he has admitted that the department has for many years been collecting fees illegally from the fishermen of this country, and his department through him now comes to this parliament and asks us to ratify what has been on 
its part an illegal act for a great many years. That is precisely what we can understand from the minister's language and from what he has read as handed to him by the deputy of the Minister of Justice. It seems to me, if that is true, that before the minister brings down such ratifying legislation the least he might do is to ask himself, or perhaps to get some word from those who are interested in the industry, as to whether it is the -proper thing to charge a licence fee for catching fish, any more than it is right to charge licence fees for growing wheat or potatoes, or cutting lumber, or making clothes. If the fishermen are to pay a licence fee, why should not everyone else pay a fee for carrying on business? Why should not the lawyers have to pay a licence fee to the federal government for charging the government $150 a day, as Peter White or Mr. Sommerville is doing? Why should the poor fisherman, who goes out in storms and winds to make $2 a day, pay a licence fee before he can catch lobsters? The minister has had a good deal of experience with the people of the country and he knows the hardships that apple growers, farmers and fishermen have to put up with. Why should he allow his officials, after stupidly collecting from fishermen for years a fee which they should not have collected, for catching lobsters or smelts, to come now and ask parliament to legalize the illegal acts of his own department? I am serious about this matter. I say to the minister that he should let it stand and investigate the matter and find out for himself what the feeling is among the fishermen in Cole harbour, Halifax county, or in Ecum Secum in my county, or in the county of the -Minister of Finance, or down in Cheti-camp, in the county of my hon. friend from Inverness, or in Glace Bay, in the county of the hon. -member for South Cape Breton, or in the county of my hon. friend from North Cape Breton? Why does he not find out the views of these people? We are much more interested, in this parliament, than are the officials of the Fisheries department, sitting in the Hunter building, to see that justice is done the fisherman, and I say to the minister in all seriousness that he should allow the bill to stand and -make a thorough investigation. I do not know how long he will be acting minister-I hope not long; I hope that -there will soon be an election so that we may have a change of government and have something done for the fisherman. But whether the minister is in charge of the department for a short or a long period, I say that before legalizing what has been an illegal act in his department for a number of

Fisheries Act
years, he should make haste slowly. He should let the bill stand and investigate the whole matter and inquire from the people who are interested in the business, whether on the Atlantic or on the Pacific, if this legislation is in the best interests of the fisheries.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 POWER TO PRESCRIBE PEES FOR FISHERY LICENCES

Within the three mile limit they certainly do belong to the people of Canada and it is not unreasonable that something should be paid for the privilege. the end. I do not think the fishermen have any great objection to this; the fees have been collected for many years, and certainly much more is spent on the fishing industry than the amount of the fees collected.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 POWER TO PRESCRIBE PEES FOR FISHERY LICENCES
speechtext: I agree with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni that the department spends certain sums of money to develop the fisheries, for fishery guardians and so forth, but my hon. friend seems to forget that where one dollar is spent on the fisheries, twenty-five dollars or more are spent, for instance, on agriculture. speechtext: Of course not. If the Minister of Agriculture were here, I would ask him to bring in a bill to make the hon. member for Comox-Alberni pay a licence fee to snare rabbits, for I understand he is a great rabbit hunter. But why should the minister collect $39,000 in amounts of 25 cents-two bits; is that the term in the west? -from the fishermen when it is not collected from farmers or apple growers in the Okanagan valley? That is what I object to. Surely the minister does not mean to suggest that fishing is the only industry upon which money is spent for its encouragement or protection. The minister must certainly know, because he is a horticulturist himself, that we vote ten times as much money for horticulture and agriculture as for fisheries- ve3, fifty times or perhaps a hundred times as much. The minister cannot get away with the story that it is necessary in order to have those few patrol boats or a few inspectors. Isn't that stupid and ridiculous? For instance in the county in which I live they have one inspector to inspect about 30,000 barrels of pickled herring and mackerel. In the city of Halifax, where perhaps 50,000 barrels come, they have two inspectors, and the minister says that because they have ;hose two inspectors in Halifax, or one in ;he constituency of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance or one in Lunenburg, they have to collect twenty-five cents from Jim Bush at La Have so that he can catch lobsters. If you put the farmers on the same basis, if you put lumbermen on the same basis, or storekeepers, all right; let us tax everyone to death. We are taxed pretty well now; there is so much paternalism and restriction that a man cannot turn around without paying a licence either to the federal or to the provincial governments. I do not know what is going to happen; the result will be that people will not try to do any business; the fishermen will not want to fish or the farmers to grow wheat or potatoes. But when the minister says to this intelligent 
body, a committee of the parliament of Canada, that it is necessary to prescribe and collect these fees because a few patrol boats or inspectors are engaged, he is not fair to himself, let alone to this parliament. As I said, fifty times as much money is voted for agriculture-and I do not say agriculture should pay a fee; as far as that is concerned I am opposed to all sorts of taxation. But why should the minister let his officials have him bring in a bill of this kind to tax the fishermen? My hon. friend says he is not trying to legalize an illegal act, but he has admitted that the collection of these fees for many years was illegal and now he is trying to legalize it.

Why make the fishermen of Inverness pay twenty-five cents for the privilege of catching lobsters? If my hon. friend wants t* pay his $400 let him pay it, but I am opposed to it; I say it is all wrong. Whether it is in connection with unemployment insurance, the eight hour day, a weekly day of rest or minimum wages, unless you can bring all the people who work with their hands and their brains under the arrangement I say this parliament should not pass it, and the same thing applies in this case. fishermea pay licence fees any mere than the farmers or any other class? That is my objection.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1932 POWER TO PRESCRIBE PEES FOR FISHERY LICENCES
speechtext: Not at all; the licence fee has nothing to do with it. We can have the 'bug professors, the fisheries inspectors and t'he apple inspectors, but why should the fishermen be the only ones to pay fees? I should like to say a word or two with respect to this matter. I am very much surprised to hear the argument of the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough with respect to fishing licences. It is only as a result of eternal vigilance on the part of the fisheries department that we have any salmon on the Pacific coast at the present time. From Alaska to the international boundary we have fishery guardians at every little cove where fish run. If it were not for that fact the fishermen would catch every fish running up those streams in any year, if they could do so. We are protecting the fishermen against themselves. I have never heard very much fault found with the licences they have to secure. They are glad to see that others are licensed, and we are expending ten dollars for every one dollar we get from the fishing industry of Canada. Fishing is not at all on a parallel with the apple industry or any other branch of agriculture. We are spending that money in order to perpetuate t'he run of the salmon. Without these licences and without supervision, which costs a good deal of money each year, I can assure you that the salmon would have been
decimated long ago on the Pacific coast. It is a fight morning, noon and night on the part of those guardians to keep purse seine men and others from going in and scooping up schools of salmon just before they ascend the streams to spawn. As I said before, the present situation is due entirely to the eternal vigilance on the part of the department, and I have nothing but good to say of what has been done by the Department of Fisheries for the fishing industry on the Pacific coats.

Mr. VENlIOT: Under this heading I wish to direct the attention of the minister to a certain occurrence in my county. I referred to it in passing, without giving details, when the Minister of Justice had a matter before the house relating to the mounted police. At the risk of being threatened with arrest or another suit for contempt of court I shall once more lodge an attack against the mounted police in connection with their enforcement of the revenue laws of the country. Early in the session I placed on the order paper the following question:
Were instructions issued by the Department of National Revenue in connection with the disposal of the vessel Paul T seized for infraction of customs regulations; if so, what were such instructions?
The answer to that question was:
Yes, to destroy the vessel.
Then the second question was as follows:
Were instructions issued' by the said department for the disposal of liquors seized on board such vessel; if so, what were such instructions?
And the answer was:
Yes, to destroy the liquor.
I am raising no objection to the destruction of smuggled liquor or the destruction of a vessel conveying smuggled liquors into Canadian waters. I would be the last one

who would wish to protect a smuggler. Having been in the civil service for some years I understand the [DOT] difficulties under which the officials of what in those days was the Department of Customs, now the Department of National Revenue, laboured in order to carry out the revenue laws. Therefore it is not my intention, nor is it to be understood that I bring the matter before the committee with any such intention, to defend those who violate our customs laws. Later in my observations I shall deal at greater length with this phase of the matter.
Turning again to my questions I find that number three is as follows:
Were instructions issued by the Department of National Revenue for the disposal of the stores found on board the Paul T; if so, what were the instructions?
The answer was that no specific instructions were given. If no specific instructions were issued in regard to the disposal of the stores, what authority had the mounted police, acting on behalf of the Department of National Revenue, to take those stores and destroy them before the people of ithe village of Shippigan? What happened? The vessel was destroyed. Late in the fall of the year she was hauled on to the bank, away from the water and clear of the ice. When the order was issued for her destruction the other vessels surrounded her on the beach, and she had to be sawn in two and afterwards burned. The machinery on that vessel, .an auxiliary engine worth $600, they destroyed, breaking it into pieces with a maul. The ship's stores were placed in a house under the protection of the police. Those stores consisted of beef, barrelled beef, canned goods, flour, molasses and so on. Afterwards they were taken out of the house, brought to the beach and destroyed by fire in the presence of a hundred or a hundred and fifty people on direct relief. It is to this point that I draw the attention of the minister. If no specific instructions were issued for the destruction of the stores, what right had the mounted police to do that? I say they had no right to do it. If it were left to the judgment of the mounted police to do what they liked with the	stores-and
apparently it was-and they in turn destroyed these stores while people prayed that they be left so that they could be used to feed little children who, starving by the roadside, watched their destruction, then I must protest.
Having dealt with that angle of the matter let me now refer to the conduct of the officials who destroyed the liquor. The cargo of liquor was valued at about $20,000. It was taken from the vessel and stored in the home of a mounted police official in the village of

Supply-National Revenue
Shippigan. Three weeks after the liquor was stored there, supposedly his house was broken into and twenty-eight cases of the liquor disappeared. A search was made, and persons were placed under arrest, or attempts were made to place them under arrest, for having stolen the liquor. The officials never found out who stole it, but there is a deep seated suspicion in the district that the liquor was not stolen by the individuals upon whom they attempted to place the blame. When the loss was discovered the remaining liquor was moved from Shippigan to Bathurst, a distance of sixty-five miles, and stored in a bonded warehouse.
The order for the destruction of the liquor came at a time when ice had formed in the harbour. Instead of breaking open the cans containing the alcohol and dumping it into the harbour, the mounted police dumped the liquor on a dump heap in the town of Bathurst, leaving no one to protect it. At five o'clock in the afternoon-
Oh, oh.

When hon. members hear the full story they will not laugh. Having thrown the liquor on the dump heap, some of the bottles were broken and liquor was left in other bottles and in the tin cans which originally contained two and one-half gallons. School children returning from school visited that dump heap and as a result we had the spectacle of little children, some of them under thirteen years of age, staggering in a drunken state through the town because the mounted police had not done their duty and had not taken measures to prevent any person from obtaining access to the dump heap. Their duty was not to destroy it on the dump heap, but to destroy it in the harbour. But having chosen the dump heap I say it was their duty to give some protection and allow no person near the point of destruction until all the liquor had been absorbed into the heap. That is the reason I bring the matter to the attention of the minister.
I should like the minister to understand that while I would support anything having to do with the prevention of smuggling I would not support the conduct of officers of the department who acted as I have indicated in the present instance. The minister or his officials should know that in this instance the dominion government had no legal right to take and to destroy the liquor, nor had they any legal right to order the destruction of the vessel. The vessel never was under seizure by the dominion government. The captain of the vessel indicated that his craft was in distress at a point thirteen miles from shore. He put out his distress signals, with
the result that the government patrol boat came to his aid and towed him to Shippigan harbour. He told the officers he had a cargo of liquor aboard. His hatches were sealed, and when the vessel reached Shippigan harbour the captain and his crew were arrested under a charge lodged not by the Department of National Revenue but byf the government of the province of New Brunswick, indicating that they were charged with having liquor in their possession which had not been purchased from the liquor commission. The captain and his crew were tried. The captain was condemned and confined to gaol, and the vessel became the property of the provincial government. On an appeal to a higher court the crew were freed and the captain was held responsible. Then the Department of National Revenue steps in and enters a case against the captain for having smuggled or attempted to smuggle liquors into Canada. The first case was tried before a provincial police court magistrate under a summary conviction, but the case entered by the Department of National Revenue was tried before a county court judge and jury, and the jury brought in a verdict of not guilty. Their verdict was that the captain was not guilty of having smuggled liquors into New Brunswick. The vessel was beyond the three mile limit, and therefore when seized under the conditions I have described, the captain was not guilty of smuggling. I want to know why, after the charge laid by the department against the captain had been tried and disproved, and the captain had been given his liberty and discharged, the department ordered the destruction of that vessel. It was the place of the provincial government to act. Did the provincial government transfer its jurisdiction to the Department of National Revenue? It has got to the point, Mr. Chairman, where this case is going to become an international one. The vessel was a French vessel, and application is being made to the government of France to intervene in the matter and to bring the case before the authorities in Canada for the protection of its citizens. As I said before, I am not raising my voice on behalf of a smuggler. I am raising it against the manner in which things are carried on, and they are carried on in such a way that the conduct of the officials of the national revenue department has made this an international question.
These are the points to which I wish to direct the attention of the minister, and I hope he will have them gone into thoroughly. I am not blaming his department, but I do say that unless it can be shown that this

captain violated the customs laws the Department of National Revenue had no jurisdiction and no authority to proceed in the way they did, and in so acting illegally they have brought about an international question between Canada and the republic of France.

The following books which may be returned to the exporters at your expense are: Interviews with Foreign Workers in a Moscow Factory; Soviet Ukraine To-day; German Workers in a Moscow Factory; Bucher; The Man in Uniform; Our Foreign Policy; Ready for Defence; The Results of the First Five Year Plan; Report on the work of the Central Committee of the C.P.S.U.; Religion and the Church in the U.S.S.R.; Youth in the Soviet Union; Kolkozniki; From Stalingrad to Kusbus.
The weight of these books is two and a half pounds, and' the return postage rates are one cent per two ounces book rate or $1.32 for the two and a half pounds, parcel post rate, as quoted by the post office here. Will you kindly advise what you wish done with these and also kindly furnish us with the name and address of the exporters?

Were these books in
English?

These were apparently in English; I am going entirely by the letter. My point is this. What protection has any Canadian citizen or any importer in a matter of this kind? I am not at all familiar with any of these books, but from the titles I cannot see any very real distinction between the books that are allowed to come in and those that are forbidden. The books in one list are allowed in and the others are not only forbidden but the return postage on them must be paid by the importer. It seems to me that the least that can be done is to inform the public what books are banned; then we should know enough not to import them. But when we are not informed as to what books are banned

Supply-National Revenue
and we send an order, then find that they are banned and that we are required to pay return postage, it is a very unfair arrangement indeed. Who is responsible for prohibiting this second list from coming in, and on what principle are they banned when the books on the first list are allowed in?

The department has
an examiner of publications who issues orders in regard to the books that may be imported, and he prohibits those that are treasonable or seditious or of an immoral or indecent character. I do not come intimately into contact with the literature to which the hon. gentleman refers; consequently I do not know very much about it. The ramifications of the department are very wide and we do not publish a list of the books that are banned, but my hon. friend may come to the department at any time and talk with the examiner and see the list of books prohibited.
Mr. WOODiSWORTH:	I do not think
that solves the problem of my friend in the university who wrote me about this matter, nor of the importer in Prince George. It does not solve the problem for a thousand other people, because they have no opportunity of going to the department and finding out what books are banned.

They can go to the
nearest collector and inquire.

They send their orders from catalogues, and then there comes a letter of this kind, which seems to me to be perfectly arbitrary. Certain books are permitted and others, which from the titles are indistinguishable from those that come in, are banned. How is the importer to know when he is not permitted to see the list of those that are banned?

Before a book is
banned it is carefully examined in the department.
Mr. WOODiSWORTH: I will give another example. In the last year I have received complaints about certain literature, again from Russia. Several years ago, shortly after I had been in Russia for a few weeks, I stopped in London and ordered a weekly paper from Russia to keep in touch with what was going on there. I have not continued my subscription but was interested at the time. I have no complaint to make because my copy of this weekly paper came through without trouble, but a number of my friends across the country have written me that their copies have been held up in the mails. There is something wrong there;
52582-105*
either some over zealous man in the postal service is exceeding his authority or else the instructions given from head office are not sufficiently clear. 'Coming to my main point, I do think that there ought to be sent out some sort of list of books that are banned so that people will know. Certainly they should not be regarded as breaking the law or be put to the inconvenience and expense of returning books that are banned when they do not know what books are banned.

I can only assure my hon. friend that we do the best we can in the circumstances. Someone has to take responsibility for the class of literature that comes in, and that responsibility belongs for the time being to my department. We are as generous as we can be as we are in all things, and I regret if the hon. gentleman has been put to any inconvenience.
Mr. WOODiSWORTH: This is not personal; Of have not been.

Well his friends may have been. I assure him that we will do everything we can to facilitate matters for them so long as the literature comes within the law and is of a class that can be properly admitted. We do not publish the list, but if he will come to the department he will find the officers courteous, kind and willing to do everything they can to assist him.
Will the minister explain the increase of $98,500, approximately ten per cent over last year?

It might be cleared up if I answered item by item. The first item is an increase of $12,000, which is explained as follows. Owing to the necessity of having sufficient funds to meet increased expenditure in connection with cartage, travelling and living expenses of relieving officers, removal expenses of officers transferred, overtime, purchase of land; and sundry small items, an increase has been provided in contingencies amounting to $71,577. From this increase of $71,577 deduct the saving in salaries which has been brought about by reduction in staff, (forty-three officers), provisional promotions without salary increase and appointments to positions at lower salaries than paid previous occupants, amounting to $59,577, and this leaves a net increase of $12,000. The second item deals with expenses of investigation, audit, preventive service. The increase here is $55,010 and it is explained as follows. Twenty additional excise tax auditors; two additional stenograph*
Supply-National Revenue

ers in the audit branch; one cashier and computing clerk transferred from the staff at the port of Winnipeg to the audit branch; four
investigators of drawback claims; two customs excise clerks; four typists, grade 2; amount required to meet travelling expenses ol additional auditors and investigators of drawback claims, making a total of $71,560. That is the gross increase. From the gross increase of $71,560 deduct the saving in salaries of positions not filled permanently, and the saving in salaries of persons appointed or promoted at lower salaries than their predecessors received, amounting to $16,550, leaving a net increase of $55,010. The next item is miscellaneous, and here the increase is $60,000. The increase in this instance is due to the necessity of providing sufficient funds t,o cover our requirements in stamps and labels and for the replacement of typewriters, adding machines and cash registers which cannot be further repaired. I would 'be glad to give the details of this appropriation, but the large items are for stamps and1 labels, $300,000, and for printing, $100,000. The others are small. That accounts for the total increase of $93,510.

I was in error when I said that the increase was ten per cent, because the total vote is $9,731,000. It is practically one per cent and it is a good deal of money. The minister however has explained the increase. Has he any other item than this, or does this complete his department?
We have no other item in the main estimates. There may be one in the supplementaries, but as to that I do not know at present.

May I revert for a moment to the question that was put to the minister by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre? Would he give us the name of the official censor in the department who passes on this literature?
Mr. J. S. Roe.

There is a case I would like
to draw to the minister's attention in connection with the collection of the sales tax as affecting a small brick plant close to where I live. This small plant has an investment of some $15,000 and employs thirtyifive meet. It has had its books regularly audited for some six years, and every year after the audit it has paid the tax computed by the officials who went through its books. But two years ago the taxing officials said: "We have made a mistake and want to go through your books

again, because we believe we should have charged you a higher tax. They made two audits of the books and claimed that the brick plant should have contributed more money by way of sales tax. The company resisted the claim successfully and the matter was dropped. But last year along came officials from the same department saying: "We want to look over your books again; we are going to go through them in another form this time and probably we will find out then what was wrong with the amount which you have paid to the department." This company claims that what has taken place has amounted to persecution; that it takes about four months to make an audit, and that it is impossible to say at the moment what price was charged on the bricks sold, because as a matter of fact many of the bricks were sold on what is called a barter basis, that is, men providing labour or wood and in return getting bricks. But the company is now compelled to go out of business owing, as it claims, to the work of these officials. They say:
The utter impossibility of a small industry paying up six years' penalties and arrears of sales tax long after the government's own assessment, based on its own audit, had been satisfied, is such that we have no recourse but to go out of business and wind up the company.
Has the minister any information regarding this plant? The name is the Vancouver Brick and Tile Company, and it was located at Sullivan, a place about eleven miles from the city of New Westminster. I feed that the officials have been over officious in this regard and that there is some ground for complaint. Has the minister received any complaints?

I have no personal
knowledge of this company. I may be wrong, but I am under the impression that there is an interlocking arrangement; and that we have had difficulty in getting at the facts and the proper values. I do not however say that as a statement of fact, but I should be very glad to review this case and talk it over with my hon. friend if he cares to come and see me about it. In that branch of the department we audit the books of 22,000 firms. I cannot undertake to retain in my memory the results of all these audits, but I shall be glad to look into the matter.

I understand from the company itself that protests were made to the minister's department and also to the hon. member for East Kootenay, and little action was taken regarding their complaint. Now they have gone out of business due to this.

Supply-National Revenue
They say that there are about 60,000 invoices to go through and some 300,000 delivery slips, because the output of the plant is sold in small lots. If that kind of thing is going on throughout the length and breadth of this country, I am afraid it will shut down a good many of the plants. I should be glad if the minister would look into the whole matter and give me an answer as to what it was that necessitated three audits by these officials.
I can only repeat that I shall be very glad to review the case. I cannot say anything more about it at the moment.

May I
ask the minister if he will do the same thing in regard to the Shenahan Company of Vancouver l He will recall the correspondence. Will he either review the case or give me an opportunity of discussing it on the supplementary estimates?
I wrote a very complete letter on this subject to my hon. friend to-day and sent it to him by hand. I hope he has received it.
Not yet.

There are many complaints
that United States firms are taking money out of Canada. I should like to make some inquiries of the minister. How many Canadians have incomes of over $50,000 a year? Hitherto it has always been over 600. This year he has reported that there are 390. I would like to know why there is this great reduction. I would also like to know how many there are in Canada who have incomes of from $200,000 to $400,000. It is felt that companies in Canada in many cases are being bled by Wall street, and some information as to the facts would be of interest; we would like to know if we are maintaining our own with the people of Wall street. It is not the desire to interfere with any individual or mention any names, but the numbers might be given of those with incomes between $200,000 and $400,000.

My hon. friend is quite correct in saying that in Canada there are 390 persons with incomes of more than $50,000 a year. But how many have an income of $200,000 or $400,000, if any, I cannot say. If the hon. member will allow me I shall be pleased to look into the matter.

Have members of the Royal
Canadian Mounted Police working in conjunction with the minister's department the authority or right to set a valuation on goods
smuggled into Canada and charge duty on that valuation? Suppose for instance a man is caught with a bicycle smuggled in from across the line-this is just a hypothetical case -and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police found him with it; in such a case are they permitted by the department to place a valuation upon the bicycle and collect duty on that valuation, or should they take him before the proper customs official in order that a proper valuation may be placed upon it?
Is my hon. friend speaking of the smuggling into the country of a bicycle or any other article and then its discovery by the police?
Yes.

In that event I am
afraid the article would be seized and forfeited under the law.

I have two cases in mind that perhaps I shall bring up later. One was in connection with a radio; the man was haled before the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, who placed a valuation on the radio and he paid duty on that valuation. I was wondering if that is a common practice.

We would require to
have full particulars. There are entries running in number to two million a year in customs and excise. If my hon. friend will give me the particulars he will receive a complete answer.
Have any sums been collected by the income tax department as a result of revelations before the price spreads and mass buying commission, and if so what is the amount?

I am informed that
the answer is no; no amount has been collected.

The mounted police
from time to time seize slot machines that are being operated illegally. I have a report that many of these machines have been brought into Canada without payment of duty. When a machine is seized for being operated illegally, an order is usually made that the machine be destroyed. Does the minister's department still proceed against the man who had that machine in his possession and collect the duty?

I am informed that if the police seize the machine under such circumstances they destroy it.
.Supply-National Revenue

But do you also collect the duty? The reason it is seized and confiscated and destroyed is because the criminal law is being broken, but that does not affect the Department of National Revenue. If the machine was brought into the country illegally then it seems to me that whoever has it in his possession should be proceeded against for the duty that should have been paid.
In that case he loses the machine, but there is no duty collected.

I ask the minister if that is a fair proposition. These machines have become a menace in various parts _ of Canada, and the police are having great difficulty in enforcing the law against them. Ostensibly the machines are for selling chewing gum or some other article, 'but frequently they are changed so as to pay nickels or quarters instead of mints and gum. I understand, that many hundreds of these machines were imported illegally, no duty having been paid on them. When they are confiscated by the police as gambling devices they are destroyed. But my point is that they are de-troyed under the criminal code, and that should not affect the right of the department to collect the duty that should have been paid. They are brought into the country in the first place as legal machines, but are used illegally. I think any one harbouring a machine^ of that kind should be responsible for finding out whether the duty has been paid before he takes the machine into bis possession.
If they come in legally the duty must have been paid.

I think we are at cross purposes as to the word "legally." They are legal machines in the sense that they can be operated legally, but they are illegal when operated contrary to the provisions of the criminal code, in other words, when they become gambling devices. My point is that owing to the difficulty the police are experiencing in controlling the operation of these machines, the department khould assist by tracing every machine back to ascertain whether or not the duty has been paid, and if not, fine the individual who is harbouring it. I ask the minister to consider that question and see if his department cannot help the various police forces in Canada in that way. I believe it would restrain those who are inclined to take such machines into their possession if they knew that in addition to losing the machine they may also have to pay the duty.

I can only repeat what I said before; if I have full particulars I shall look into it. We are continually following goods that have been smuggled into the country. But if any machine is brought in duty paid and then operated illegally I am afraid it is not a matter for my department.
I appreciate that, but the report is that most of these machines are smuggled into the country in the first place.
That is just a general report?
That is a general report, and I would like to know if the minister has any information to give the committee in that connection.
I have no information, but certainly I will investigate the matter.

These machines are
being seized by the police all the time, an odd one here and there, and it seems to me it is a matter that should be looked into by the department.

The minister will recall
that when his estimates were before the committee a year ago there were certain questions pending with regard to the powers of the tariff board and certain rulings given by them. Have any fresh disputes arisen which have been submitted to the supreme court since that time?
No.

It has been drawn to
my attention that it is impossible for a person to buy a car in the United States and import it into Canada. I should like to ask if that condition exists to-day.

There is nothing to
prevent a person from buying a car in the United States and bringing it into Canada, on paying the duty, so long as it is not a used car.
What do you mean by a used car? How long must it be used to become a used car?
A used car is one not manufactured during the current calendar year.

Then I should like to
place a case before the minister, that of a Canadian citizen temporarily in the United States who buys an automobile which he drives for eight or ten days. Then he crosses the border. Is it possible for him to bring

Supply-National Revenue
that new car, which he has driven for a week or ten days, into Canada if he pays the duty?
Certainly.

I should like to
ask a question in connection with this matter of cars. When I was in Chicago last Easter I saw a Chrysler car advertised for $495. When I came back to Ottawa I saw the same type of Chrysler car selling for something around $900. Will the minister explain che reason for that difference in price? What elements enter into the price of the car in Canada? If that is the same car I saw here in Ottawa I should like to buy it in the United States and bring it here, because I would save about $200 or $300 by doing so.

I suggest that the minister
invite the hon. member to see him in his office to-morrow in order to discuss the matter fully.

I should like to ask the minister a question with regard to the regulations issued to the collectors of customs. In the case to which I am referring a man bought a radio in the United States. It came to the customs in the ordinary way and he paid the customs duty, which I presume was levied according to the instructions issued to the collector at that port. Six months later he received a letter from the collector saying there was $40 more to pay on the radio. It seems to me that when that person bought that radio in good faith and had it shipped in the ordinary way, paying the duty demanded at the time it arrived in the country, he should not be asked to pay an additional sum six months later. I should like the minister to explain how such a thing can occur. It seems ridiculous, but I know it to be a fact. I should like to know if the customs officers can collect an additional duty six months or a year later.
If my hon. friend will give me the name and the port of entry I will certainly investigate.

The port of entry was Prince Rupert. I do not know the name, but I shall be only too glad to secure it, because I know that occurred last year; the man was asked to pay an additional duty six months after he received the goods. If the minister will take up the matter I will secure the information and see him later.
Certainly.

I should like to ask one other question in connection with our old friend gasoline. Some time ago the fixing of values for duty purposes was done away with. In the importation of gasoline from the United States are there any imposts other than the duty of 2J cents a gallon?
There is the special excise tax and also the sales tax.
Anything else? Is there anything in the way of dumping duty in addition to the 2| cents per gallon?

That would depend
upon the facts of the case, after investigation. If the gasoline is being dumped of course the dumping duty would apply.
Has the minister any record of recent imposition of dumping duties on gasoline brought in from the United States?
There may have been but I could not tell without looking it up. There is no fixed value. No general action has been taken, but there may have been a particular case.
I would be able to get that information by writing the department?
Yes.

It is not clear in my mind yet as to just how the duty is applied on a car imported from the United States. I am a private citizen of Canada; I go to the United States and buy a new car, which I run for five, seven or ten days. Then I come to the port of entry. I want the minister to tell me the duty that must be paid on that car by me, a private citizen, and if there is any difference between that and the duty paid by an importer of cars.

In the instance given by my hon. friend he would pay the duty on the retail list price. In the other case, if my hon. friend is referring to a dealer in cars, the dealer would pay the same rate of duty on the list price less twenty per cent.

Then am I to understand from the answer given by the minister that it is possible for me, a private citizen of Canada, to import from the United States a new car that has been used for five, seven or ten days and, on paying the duty, bring it in to Canada as a new car? Can I do that as a private citizen?

Yes. I think I gave that information to the hon. gentleman a few moments ago. He can do that.
Supply-National Revenue
Is it correct in practice? Does your department permit that?
The commissioner of customs says we are doing it every day.

I do not like to mention specific cases, but I know of a specific case where a private citizen of Canada was not permitted to import a car from the United States. I think the minister's officials at least have knowledge of the case. It was a new car, used for perhaps about seven days before the attempt to import it into Canada.
Was this a reicent case?
Quite recent, yes.
If the member will give me the facts in confidence I shall be pleased to look into them.

A friend of mine received a Christmas present from Europe, consisting of a cigarette lighter which cost about 30 cents, or, as the invoice which I have in my possession indicates, one krone and ten ore. He received a letter indicating that the gift had been forwarded to him, and when it arrived at the customs office he was asked to come down and clear it. Before he could get it out of the hands of the customs officials he had to pay $1.76, for which I hold the receipt. How could any customs official arrive at that amount as the duty payable on an article of that value? How do they set their valuations? Is it a dumping duty or some other kind of duty?

A Christmas duty.
Mr. HANiSON (Skeena): I should like to know how the amount would be arrived at, especially in view of the fact that the invoice was sent with the lighter, and that a receipt was given for the amount paid to the customs.
A burning shame.
I do not know what to say about that. I cannot conceive of a duty being imposed such as the hon. member has mentioned.
i can produce the receipt and the lighter.

I can scarcely credit so high a duty on an article costing 30 cents. However, there are 5,500 employees in the department, and of course the human element will enter into all matters of administration. Sometimes mistakes are made. But I shall 	,|
be very glad to look into the matter, I should like to have the document the hon. member mentioned.
I shall give it to the minister.

In the opinion of the minister or the officials in front of him, how long has a citizen of Canada visiting the United States and buying a car there to be the possessor of it before it is considered second hand, for purposes of importation into Canada?
I cannot have made myself clear to the hon. member.
I do not think the minister did.

What I intended to say was this: My officials inform me that if a Canadian goes to the United States and buys a new car, no matter how far he may have driven it, he may bring it in upon payment of duty. He cannot, however, buy a second band car and import it. Is that clear?

That is not the point. Suppose a private citizen of Canada-not a dealer, but a common every day Canadian citizen-goes to the United States, buys a new car and imports it into Canada, Can he do so, no matter how far the car has travelled in the United States or how long he has had it?
Provided it is a new car, yes.
Would the minister give me a definition of a new oar?
I have given the definition twice, but I shall give it again. A new car is a car manufactured in the calendar year in which it is purchased.

And imported.
Mr. MEElQIEiR (St. Henri): That would apply even if the man used the car for six months in the United States?
Yes, certainly. H he is in the United States and buys a car this year he may use it for six months over there and then bring it in as a new car and pay duty on it.
Suppose he buys in the following December a car made in January, is it still considered a new car?

Ilf it is a new car, that is, if be buys it as a new car.

Supply-Finance
But suppose it has been used during the year by someone else?
No.
That would be a second hand car.
Suppose a ear is manufactured in December, 1934, and it is bought from the warehouse in January, 1935, would the car be new or second hand? The car I have in mind has never been out of the warehouse.
I am told that that would be prohibited importation.

I understand it makes no difference what price the private individual may pay for the car in the United States; he must pay the duty on the retail price. He may buy it at the wholesale price, but that does not make any difference 'because when he comes to the boundary line he has to pay the duty on the retail price of the car in the United States.
Mr. MATTHEW'S: Only a dealer may Obtain a dealer's discount when bringing a car in.

Suppose I go across the line and buy a car for which 1 have paid only the wholesale price, as shown by an invoice in my possession; when 1 come to the boundary line I understand I have to pay duty on the retail price. It seems to make no difference when I state the price I paid for the car.
Mr. MATTHEW'S: You pay the duty on the fair market value as sold for home consumption.

If I had gone to California last November, bought a car in that state, and came back to Canada this month, I would not be permitted to bring it into Canada, although I had driven it those three or four months?
The hon. member is quite correct.
Item agreed to.

Is it the intention of the Department of Finance to disclose to hon. members complete information with respect to the' newly formed Bank of Canada, its officers, the salaries of the
staff, and such other information as might be deemed to be in the best interests of the public service?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a comprehensive question, involving a matter of major policy. In the past we have followed a policy of marked distinction in dealing with separate bodies, although such bodies may have been set up by parliament. I should say that it would be quite fitting and proper that the salaries of the officers named in the first instance should be disclosed. But the minutiae of the cost of management, the salaries of individual employees, how much ink they use, how much sealing wax and that sort of thing-I do not use that illustration for the purpose of making the question of my hon. friend appear ludicrous, because it is a perfectly fair question; I merely carry it to that extreme point as indicating that the intimate and minute details of the management of the bank would not I think be a proper subject for inquiry and disclosure as a matter of course. That is at the moment my reaction to the question put to me by my hon. friend, but I should like to turn it over in my mind a little furtheT before I give him an official and final answer, because it is a question of policy which should be settled on a basis satisfactory to the house and to public opinion generally, rather than one which should be permitted to become a matter of controversy as to how far we should or should not go in the disclosing of information. I would prefer, therefore, that my hon. friend should not at the moment press for a minute or detailed reply to his inquiry; before the session is over I shall be quite prepared to make a statement as to government policy in the matter.
Does the salary of the superintendent in bankruptcy come under Finance?
